name: knowledgec_query
description: Read knowledgeC.db, the application and device-state records macOS keeps for its own features (not an audit log): for each ZOBJECT row its stream, typed values (value_string, value_integer, value_double, value_type_code: the lock and backlight states are integers), raw and converted start, end and creation times (Apple epoch, 2001-01-01 UTC, to ISO 8601 UTC with the raw value kept), UUID, the other non-null ZOBJECT columns and, joined on the row's own foreign keys, every non-null column of its ZSTRUCTUREDMETADATA and ZSOURCE rows under their own names. The joins are made from the schema the file has; the answer says which tables joined, lists the tables and columns and carries a fingerprint of the three tables' columns. A stream's meaning, and whether it exists, depends on the build and the device: the streams of the file are inventoried (count, first and last start) in one pass whatever the filters, and none is assumed; the list holds the 2,000 with the most entries (streams of one count cut at random), by count and, among equal counts, in the order they are printed (a withheld name's place in the list says nothing about its bytes), and the others are counted in streams_not_listed (streams_in_file is how many there are) and make the answer partial; the schema lists at most 1,000 tables, the three the tool reads always among them, and counts the rest in tables_not_listed. stream is a LIKE pattern matched against the stream name as the answer prints it, never against a name that is withheld (a count of rows for a prefix would tell a true guess of a hidden name from a false one): rows of a stream whose printed name is withheld and did not match are counted in stream_blind_rows and make the answer partial, the count being the same whatever the pattern says of what is hidden, and the pattern <withheld% selects the streams that are withheld. since and until filter by start time (a record that began earlier and overlapped the window is not selected); a filter the database has no column for is listed in filters_unapplied and the answer is partial. A write-ahead log beside the database holds committed rows the main file lacks; a rollback journal holds the old pages of a transaction that did not commit and holds no such rows (a journal that is not a valid hot journal, 3,000 random bytes say, is removed by SQLite without changing the database, and the answer says that and does not call it a rollback). With either, the files are copied to a private directory, SQLite works on the copy (WAL frames applied are counted; a hot journal is rolled back in the copy, reported in source_used.journal and in problems because the copy's state is then not the main file's), and the copy is removed, so the evidence directory is never written to; without a sidecar the file is opened read-only and immutable. What it does not measure: Biome streams, other databases, whether a screen or focus state shows a person at the keyboard (it does not), or whether the stream was complete (retention varies). Every row carries its Z_PK and parser; rows are ordered by start then Z_PK; they are written to out_file as they are read (an existing file or link there is refused), or paged losslessly to a file the answer names. Cells are read bounded, and a statement never loads a TEXT cell: a TEXT cell is read through a blob handle (on a second connection that is replaced every 20,000 handles, since CPython's sqlite3 keeps a weak reference to each handle until its connection closes), a BLOB longer than 4096 bytes is not read at all but for its head, and a TEXT or BLOB value longer than 4096 characters or bytes is returned as its first 4096, its whole byte length, _truncated and where the whole is in the database (_where: table, column, rowid): a 300 MB TEXT cell costs about 30 MB of memory, not 324. A BLOB's head is hexadecimal (_hex), not base64. On a Python without blob handles (before 3.11) a statement reads a TEXT cell whole. export_oversize: true, in a job run as secret output, streams each whole value to a private file (mode 0600) under $OUT/tool-output/knowledgec-values/ and names it (max_export_bytes bounds the total). The inline answer is cut at max_inline_bytes as well as at limit, and a rerun that finds fewer rows does not replace a larger earlier page file (it writes a new name and says which it kept). A schema it cannot read (a virtual table whose module is missing), a ZOBJECT with no ZSTREAMNAME and an unapplied filter are named in problems and the answer is partial. The tool has a clock of its own, max_seconds (default 80, at most 90, below the 120 seconds of the manifest; the answer's sealing, up to 10 seconds, and the stream inventory, up to 8, come after it; the inventory, the judging of its names and their listing are all inside those 8 seconds, and a file of 1,000,000 distinct stream names ends in 11.6 s with max_seconds 10, 81.5 s on the default 80 and 94.4 s (3,000,000 names) with max_seconds 90 and rows enough to use it, in 91 to 178 MB; before it took 84.7 s and 127.7 s (past the 120 s of the manifest) and 810 MB): a progress handler aborts the statement when it passes, so even the sort of a table with millions of rows is stopped, the copy of a database with a sidecar is stopped by it too (nothing is read, and the copy is removed), and the clock is read at every row (the row in hand is judged first: rows of 40 strings of 4,000 characters take a fifth of a second each, and the clock was read every 256 rows, which ran max_seconds 20 to 49.8 seconds). When it passes, or a stop signal arrives, status is partial, the entries are a prefix of the result in start order (the whole prefix is in the file the answer names, and out_file is kept), and resume gives rows_read, stopped_after_z_pk, last_start_raw, after_start_raw and after_z_pk, the two arguments to run again with: the read goes on at the next row of the order (start, then Z_PK), no row twice and none skipped, also when thousands of rows share one start (resume_since, a microsecond before the last start, is the older way and reads the rows of that start again, which can stop at the same 4,096 rows for ever). SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGHUP end it the same way: one JSON answer with interrupted set to the signal's name, exit 128 plus the signal, the staged copy of the database removed. A stop signal that arrives while the answer is being sealed (up to 10 seconds, with a large preview) waits for the answer and is named in it: interrupted is set, status is partial and the exit code is 128 plus the signal. A signal that arrives while the text of the answer is being made or written (a few tenths of a second for an answer of 20 to 44 MB) cannot be put into a text that is already out: it is found afterwards, the exit code is still 128 plus the signal and stderr says that the answer on stdout is whole and was not marked (before this, 2 of 18 signals sent in that window to knowledgec_query and 2 of 14 to fsevents_parse ended with exit code 0 and an answer that said complete). SIGKILL cannot be handled. The private copy is created with mode 0600 in a directory named for the process (knowledgec-<pid>-...) that holds a lock file the process keeps locked until it ends; the copy that a SIGKILL leaves is removed by the next run in that place when that lock is free (a live run's is never touched, one of another PID namespace that shares the place included, and a process number that has been reused does not keep a dead run's copy). A database whose schema holds text that is not UTF-8 (SQLite's own error message then cannot be decoded) is a JSON refusal, not a traceback. Every answer and refusal carries status (complete, partial or failed) and status_basis. out_file is created with mode 0600. SENSITIVE: the values, URLs (a Safari history or web-usage value can carry a token in its query string), bundle and device ids, other columns and a BLOB's head are evidence text. WITHHOLDING (one boundary on every way out, with two checks of the tool's own around it). The windows-forensics pack's shared boundary block, copied byte for byte (a test holds the copies equal), judges every key and value of the answer, of an error answer, and of every row of every file this tool writes, by the type of the field it fills: a name, path, key or URL is shown as it is only when it fits a plain grammar (a path component by component; GUIDs, SIDs, addresses, 0x numbers, times and hexadecimal ids up to 24 digits are plain); free text has token-shaped runs, user-info, the value after a secret's name, vendor-prefixed tokens, padded base64 and PEM keys withheld; and a second check, written apart from the first, reads it all once more, the text as the evidence wrote it as well as the text shown (a string it replaces makes a complete answer partial and is listed under boundary.replaced_at). A withheld text is <withheld N characters: reason>. Past the judging time (10 seconds for an answer or a row, and never past the seal stop of the tool) the strings the evidence supplied are no longer judged: each is replaced whole and the answer is partial, except the names this tool wrote itself and a string of 15 characters or fewer made only of letters, digits, _ and . that does not start like a vendor token. write_values: true writes the originals of everything the boundary withheld to knowledgec_query-values.jsonl under $OUT (mode 0600, created first, never replaced); it and export_oversize are accepted only in a job the harness runs as secret output (the manifest declares both; SECRET_OUTPUT=1), refused as JSON anywhere else before anything is made. Measured on random plants in a value, in another ZOBJECT column, in a BLOB's head, in a UUID and as the name of a column (rates, not guarantees; a second measurement planted 1,000 per shape and slot, and tests/pack-macos-forensics-boundary.test.ts plants 300 per shape and asserts the bounds). Of the 21 shapes the boundary claims (GitHub, GitLab, Stripe, SendGrid, Google and npm tokens, AWS key ids, JWT, PEM private keys, user-info with an @ in the password, Password= and password: values, NUL and zero-width splits, base64 keys of 16, 20 and 32 bytes, AWS-shaped keys of 40 characters, random base62 of 24 and 40 characters) 19 were printed whole in 0 of 1,000 plants in every slot; an AWS-shaped key of 40 characters in 1 of 1,000 (a value, and a BLOB's head when the key holds a /) and random base62 of 24 characters in 1 to 4 of 1,000; a piece of 12 characters of an AWS-shaped key and of a random base62 token was printed in 1 to 3 of 1,000 plants. Two checks of the tool's own surround the boundary, which is the windows pack's block and is not edited here: the hexadecimal of a field (a BLOB's head, a UUID) is read once more with the NULs and the invisible characters taken out, in UTF-8 and in UTF-16 (a token cut by a NUL, by an invisible character (format characters, combining marks, private-use and unassigned code points, fillers) or by a control character every 15 characters or fewer shows no run that looks like a secret in the bytes as they are; each control character that occurs in the text is also taken out alone, one at a time, because taking all of them out at once joins the printable bytes of random data into runs; a token cut by two or more different control characters is not read through; a field so long and so full of control characters that this would take over 2 million characters of reading, about 64 KB of random bytes, is withheld), and is withheld when that text holds a secret-shaped run; and a FileVault personal recovery key (six groups of four capitals and digits joined by -) is withheld by a rule of its own. Before them a token cut by a NUL or a zero-width character every 6, 12 or 15 characters was printed whole in the hexadecimal of a BLOB's head in 1,000 of 1,000 plants, of a BLOB's long head in 990 to 996 and of a UUID in 1,000 (the same token in a text field in 0 of 1,000); after them 0 of 200 in each of the three slots, and 0 of 100 random 256-byte BLOBs withheld (in 4 KB of random bytes the block alone withholds about 0.6%, for a user-info-like run). A token cut by a control character (U+0001, DEL, ESC, NEL), a private-use or an unassigned code point every 6 characters was printed whole in the hexadecimal of a BLOB's head and of a UUID in 200 of 200 plants each (the same token in a text field in 0 of 200); in-process, 23 shapes cut every 6, 12, 15, 16 and 20 characters were printed in 460, 417, 359, 143 and 73 of 460; after the checks 0 of 200 in each slot and 0 of 460 at every distance. The checks' cost, on 300 real file heads of 4 KB (one Mac's /Applications, /System/Library, /usr/lib, /Library and /usr/share): the block alone withholds 113, the checks 6 more (3 before this change); on 300 binary property list heads 178 and 2 more (1 before); on 1,000 random blobs of 256 bytes 0 and 0, of 4 KB 6 and 4 more (0 before); private-use and unassigned code points alone added 0 of 300 and 0 of 1,000. A token written as spaced hexadecimal, as percent escapes, zlib-compressed or reversed is printed in a BLOB's head as it is in a text field (690, 690, 679 and 98 of 690 plants): the boundary does not claim these shapes and the checks do not read them. A FileVault recovery key was printed in 29 to 32% of plants in a value, a stream and a BLOB's head, in 8% (25 of 300) as the head of a BLOB longer than 4096 bytes and in 30% (30 of 100) as a table name; after the rule, which looks for the six groups wherever they stand, also next to other letters or digits, 0 of 300 in a value, a stream, a BLOB's head, a long BLOB's head and a text longer than 4096 characters, and 0 of 100 as a table name (table names pass the rule too); a key inside a column name is not covered (26 of 100 plants printed). The id of a user's temporary folder in a path (/var/folders/xx/ and 30 characters) that the block would withhold is shown as tmp-id- and 12 hexadecimal digits of its sha256: the same id is the same alias in every run and in every tool. The shapes it does not claim are printed: a plain password, a four-word passphrase and a UUID-shaped key, 1,000 of 1,000; a BitLocker recovery key (eight groups of six digits), 1,000 of 1,000; a random token of 16 characters with spaces or - _ . among them (a Wi-Fi password) in 35 to 67% of plants; random base62 of 16 characters in 0.4 to 1.0%, of 20 in 0.1 to 0.9%, of 32 in 0.1 to 0.2%; text written as spaced characters, as HTML entities, as hexadecimal with spaces or as percent escapes in a text field, 1,000 of 1,000. The 47 column names of a knowledgeC schema written from Apple's CoreData naming pass unchanged; no real knowledgeC database was at hand to measure what it costs on one. NOT recognised, by design: a secret that does not look like one (a plain password or passphrase, a pronounceable passphrase, a UUID-shaped key, a hexadecimal secret of up to 24 digits in a name, random bytes with no text in them, anything under 16 characters in a name): withholding is by shape, so a file whose secrets matter is read in a job run with secret_output: true. Strings the shape rules change that are not secrets: numbers of 19 digits or more, unlabelled hexadecimal runs of 32 digits or more, and the query values of a URL. Column names are shown (the names of a real knowledgeC schema pass).

db.description: A knowledgeC.db; any -wal, -shm or -journal beside it is used (in a private copy), so copy them out together

stream.description: A stream name or a LIKE pattern (case-insensitive; % and _ are wildcards), e.g. '/app/inFocus' or '/app/%'. It is matched against the stream name as the answer prints it, never against one that is withheld: rows of a withheld stream that it did not match are counted in stream_blind_rows (the answer is partial); '<withheld%' selects the withheld streams

since.description: Only entries starting at or after this ISO 8601 UTC time (needs a ZSTARTDATE column; otherwise listed in filters_unapplied)

until.description: Only entries starting at or before this ISO 8601 UTC time (same)

limit.description: Entries shown inline (default 500). All are counted; the whole result is in out_file, or, when that is omitted, in a file under work/<your id>/tool-output/ (in a job, $OUT/tool-output/) that the answer names

out_file.description: JSONL path for every matching entry (each row judged by the boundary), written as each is read, mode 0600. The tool does not overwrite: an existing file or link at that name is refused

max_stage_bytes.description: The database and its sidecars are copied only up to this many bytes in all (default 2147483648); over it nothing is read and the answer says so

max_inline_bytes.description: The inline entries are cut at this many bytes as well as at `limit` entries (default 1048576); the whole is in out_file or the file the answer names

export_oversize.description: Write each TEXT or BLOB value longer than 4096 characters or bytes, whole, to a private file under $OUT/tool-output/knowledgec-values/ and name it in the cell. Only in a job run with secret_output: true, refused anywhere else; default false

max_export_bytes.description: export_oversize writes at most this many bytes in all (default 1073741824); a value that would pass it is not written and the answer says so

max_seconds.description: The tool's own clock (default 80, at most 90): read at every row, and while a database with a sidecar is copied; when it passes the read stops, status is partial and resume says how to go on; a larger value is clamped and the answer says so

write_values.description: Write the originals of everything the boundary withheld to $OUT/knowledgec_query-values.jsonl (mode 0600, created first, never replaced): only in a job run with secret_output: true, refused anywhere else; default false

after_z_pk.description: Go on after the row with this Z_PK in the order (start, then Z_PK), together with after_start_raw: both are resume.after_z_pk and resume.after_start_raw of a run that stopped. No row is read twice or skipped, also when many rows share one start. Given without after_start_raw it is refused, as is a number SQLite cannot hold (over 64 bits)

after_start_raw.description: The raw start (Apple epoch) of the last row a stopped run read, with after_z_pk; null when that row had no start. A number SQLite cannot hold (an integer over 64 bits) is refused
